trig-complex-polar-rectangular-complex-n.title: Rectangular complex-number form
trig-complex-polar-rectangular-complex-n.summary: Represent a complex number as a+bi, perform exact arithmetic and division with conjugates, and distinguish real and imaginary components.

blocks.text: A complex number z=a+bi has real part a and imaginary part b, where a,b are real and i²=−1. The imaginary part is b (a real number), not bi. Add and subtract like components; to divide, multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the divisor.

blocks.caption: Original complex-plane illustration showing Cartesian geometry, argument or rotational symmetry; for exact numerical positions always use the written formulas.

blocks.title: Simplify (3+2i)(1−4i)
blocks.strategy: Distribute all terms and replace i² by −1.
blocks.check: Check the real part: 3+8=11; imaginary part: −12+2=−10.

blocks.title: Divide (5+3i) by (1−i)
blocks.strategy: Multiply by the denominator’s complex conjugate.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Never treat i² as +1; keep the divisor nonzero. The imaginary part of 5+3i is 3, not 3i.

blocks.explanation: Conjugation changes only the sign of the imaginary coefficient, so the real part remains −2.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Lial et al., Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§8.1–8.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §5.3; Moyer and Ayres, Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 15; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Ch. 18. Euler and phasor examples use standard complex-analysis/electrical-engineering conventions; phase sign conventions depend on the time convention chosen.

trig-complex-polar-the-complex-plane.title: The complex plane
trig-complex-polar-the-complex-plane.summary: Locate complex numbers on the Argand plane, recognize conjugation as reflection, and interpret vector addition geometrically.

blocks.text: Plot z=x+iy as the point (x,y) on the complex plane: the horizontal axis is real and the vertical axis imaginary. Complex addition adds coordinate vectors. Conjugation reflects a point across the real axis. The origin corresponds to z=0.

blocks.caption: Original complex-plane illustration showing Cartesian geometry, argument or rotational symmetry; for exact numerical positions always use the written formulas.

blocks.title: Plot z=−3+4i and its conjugate
blocks.strategy: Use the real coordinate as x and the imaginary coefficient as y.
steps: Plot z at (−3,4), in quadrant II.
Its conjugate −3−4i is at (−3,−4), in quadrant III.
blocks.check: Both points are equally far from the real axis; reflection keeps x unchanged.

blocks.title: Add z₁=2+i and z₂=−4+3i graphically
blocks.strategy: Combine horizontal and vertical displacements separately.
steps: Imaginary components: 1+3=4, so the resultant point is (−2,4), or −2+4i.
blocks.check: The tail-to-head addition of vectors produces the same resultant.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Do not place bi on the horizontal real axis or mistake conjugation for negating both components.

blocks.explanation: The real coordinate −2 and imaginary coordinate −3 are both negative, identifying quadrant III.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Lial et al., Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§8.1–8.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §5.3; Moyer and Ayres, Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 15; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Ch. 18. Euler and phasor examples use standard complex-analysis/electrical-engineering conventions; phase sign conventions depend on the time convention chosen.

trig-complex-polar-modulus-and-argument.title: Modulus and argument
trig-complex-polar-modulus-and-argument.summary: Calculate modulus and principal argument with correct quadrants, and explain why z=0 has no defined argument.

blocks.text: For z=x+iy, the modulus is its distance from the origin. An argument is any angle θ satisfying cosθ=x/|z| and sinθ=y/|z|. For nonzero z, arguments differ by 2π. We use the principal convention Arg z∈(−π,π]; atan2(y,x) resolves the quadrant and gives −π for the negative real axis in some software, which we report as +π.

blocks.caption: Original complex-plane illustration showing Cartesian geometry, argument or rotational symmetry; for exact numerical positions always use the written formulas.

blocks.title: Find |−3+4i| and its principal argument
blocks.strategy: Compute the norm and quadrant-II reference angle.
steps: The quadrant-II principal angle is π−arctan(4/3), approximately 126.87°.

blocks.title: Find the principal argument of −2−2i
blocks.strategy: Use quadrant III, then convert to a signed principal angle.
steps: Subtract 360° to obtain principal Arg z=−135°=−3π/4.
blocks.check: Cos(−135°) and sin(−135°) are both negative, as required.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: The ordinary arctan(y/x) misses quadrant information. The argument of zero is undefined; the negative real axis maps to +π in the chosen principal convention.

Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Lial et al., Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§8.1–8.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §5.3; Moyer and Ayres, Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 15; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Ch. 18. Euler and phasor examples use standard complex-analysis/electrical-engineering conventions; phase sign conventions depend on the time convention chosen.

trig-complex-polar-polar-and-trigonometr.title: Polar and trigonometric forms
trig-complex-polar-polar-and-trigonometr.summary: Convert between rectangular and trigonometric forms using quadrant-aware arguments, and include the zero-number exception.

blocks.text: Every nonzero complex number can be written in trigonometric form r(cosθ+i sinθ), with r=|z|>0 and θ an argument. This is also abbreviated r cis θ. Rectangular components are x=r cosθ and y=r sinθ. For z=0, set r=0; no unique argument exists.

blocks.caption: Original complex-plane illustration showing Cartesian geometry, argument or rotational symmetry; for exact numerical positions always use the written formulas.

blocks.title: Convert −1+i to trigonometric form
blocks.strategy: Determine radius and argument using its quadrant.
steps: Its argument is 135°=3π/4; hence z=√2(cos135°+i sin135°).
blocks.check: The result has real part −1 and imaginary part +1.

blocks.title: Convert 6 cis(−π/6) into rectangular form
blocks.strategy: Apply cosine and sine component relationships.
blocks.check: Modulus √(27+9)=6, consistent with the given polar radius.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: A negative radius is not needed in the standard r≥0 convention. State degree or radian units; never assign a unique angle to z=0.

blocks.prompt: What is 4 cis(π/2) in rectangular form?
blocks.explanation: cos(π/2)=0 and sin(π/2)=1, so the real component vanishes.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Lial et al., Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§8.1–8.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §5.3; Moyer and Ayres, Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 15; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Ch. 18. Euler and phasor examples use standard complex-analysis/electrical-engineering conventions; phase sign conventions depend on the time convention chosen.

trig-complex-polar-multiplication-and-di.title: Multiplication and division in polar form
trig-complex-polar-multiplication-and-di.summary: Multiply and divide nonzero complex numbers by multiplying/dividing moduli and adding/subtracting arguments.

blocks.text: In polar form, multiplication adds phases and multiplies magnitudes; division subtracts phases and divides magnitudes. This follows from trigonometric addition formulas. Division is only defined if the divisor is nonzero. Reduce the resulting angle modulo 2π when requested.

blocks.caption: Original complex-plane illustration showing Cartesian geometry, argument or rotational symmetry; for exact numerical positions always use the written formulas.

blocks.title: Multiply (2 cis30°)(3 cis75°)
blocks.strategy: Multiply moduli and add angles, retaining degrees.
steps: Argument: 30°+75°=105°, so the product is 6 cis105°.

blocks.title: Divide (8 cis150°) by (2 cis(−30°))
blocks.strategy: Divide moduli and subtract the second angle.
steps: Argument: 150°−(−30°)=180°, so the quotient is 4 cis180°=−4.
blocks.check: Multiply −4 by 2 cis(−30°) to recover 8 cis150°.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Subtract the divisor argument for division; do not divide angles. A zero divisor makes division undefined.

blocks.prompt: What is the modulus of (3 cis20°)(4 cis40°)?
blocks.explanation: Polar product multiplies the moduli: 3×4=12, regardless of the angles.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Lial et al., Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§8.1–8.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §5.3; Moyer and Ayres, Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 15; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Ch. 18. Euler and phasor examples use standard complex-analysis/electrical-engineering conventions; phase sign conventions depend on the time convention chosen.

trig-complex-polar-eulers-formula.title: Euler’s formula
trig-complex-polar-eulers-formula.summary: Relate trigonometric complex form to complex exponentials using Euler’s identity and a clear imaginary-unit convention.

blocks.text: Euler’s formula e^{iθ}=cosθ+i sinθ is valid for real θ measured in radians. It expresses rotation on the unit circle as a complex exponential; electrical engineering sometimes uses j in place of i to avoid confusion with current. If a sinusoid is represented as Re{Ae^{i(ωt+φ)}}, its instantaneous real signal is A cos(ωt+φ).

blocks.caption: Original complex-plane illustration showing Cartesian geometry, argument or rotational symmetry; for exact numerical positions always use the written formulas.

blocks.title: Evaluate e^{iπ} and e^{iπ/2}
blocks.strategy: Substitute standard angles in Euler’s identity.
blocks.check: Both outputs have modulus one, as e^{iθ} represents a rotation.

blocks.title: Interpret Re{5e^{i(100t−π/6)}}
blocks.strategy: Extract the real part of the complex exponential.
steps: The physical real signal is 5cos(100t−π/6), using a positive-frequency e^{iωt} convention.
blocks.check: Frequency is 100 rad/s; the real signal remains real valued.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Euler’s exponential uses radians. In AC engineering, verify whether e^{+jωt} or e^{−jωt} is assumed before comparing lead/lag signs; j and i denote the same imaginary unit.

Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Lial et al., Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§8.1–8.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §5.3; Moyer and Ayres, Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 15; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Ch. 18. Euler and phasor examples use standard complex-analysis/electrical-engineering conventions; phase sign conventions depend on the time convention chosen.

trig-complex-polar-de-moivres-theorem.title: De Moivre’s theorem
trig-complex-polar-de-moivres-theorem.summary: Use De Moivre’s theorem to compute positive integer powers efficiently and explain the relation to repeated rotation.

blocks.text: For an integer n≥0, De Moivre’s theorem states (cosθ+i sinθ)^n=cos(nθ)+i sin(nθ). A complex number r cisθ raised to n has modulus r^n and angle nθ. Negative powers are valid only for z≠0 and are treated by reciprocal powers.

blocks.caption: Original complex-plane illustration showing Cartesian geometry, argument or rotational symmetry; for exact numerical positions always use the written formulas.

blocks.title: Compute (1+i)⁴ by De Moivre’s theorem
blocks.strategy: Find modulus and argument before applying the power.

blocks.title: Compute (2 cis20°)³
blocks.strategy: Raise modulus to the third power, and multiply the argument by three.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: The modulus is raised to the power; the argument is multiplied by the power—not raised to it. For n<0, z must be nonzero.

Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Lial et al., Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§8.1–8.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §5.3; Moyer and Ayres, Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 15; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Ch. 18. Euler and phasor examples use standard complex-analysis/electrical-engineering conventions; phase sign conventions depend on the time convention chosen.

trig-complex-polar-powers-and-roots-of-c.title: Powers and roots of complex numbers
trig-complex-polar-powers-and-roots-of-c.summary: Calculate integer powers and all distinct nth roots of nonzero complex numbers, including roots of unity and the zero case.

blocks.text: If z=r cisθ with r>0, its n distinct nth roots (n positive integer) have modulus r^(1/n) and angles (θ+2πk)/n for k=0,…,n−1. They are equally spaced on a circle. The nth root of zero is only zero (not n distinct roots). Verify candidates by raising them to the nth power.

blocks.caption: Original complex-plane illustration showing Cartesian geometry, argument or rotational symmetry; for exact numerical positions always use the written formulas.

blocks.title: Find all cube roots of 8
blocks.strategy: Treat 8 as 8 cis0 and list all three angles.
steps: Root modulus is ∛8=2; angles are 0°, 120°, and 240°.
blocks.check: Cubing any listed root produces 8; the three roots are distinct.

blocks.title: Find all fourth roots of 16 cisπ
blocks.problem: Find all fourth roots of 16 cisπ
blocks.strategy: Divide all possible arguments by four.
steps: Angles are π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, and 7π/4; roots are 2cis of each angle.
blocks.check: The four angular positions differ by π/2, and fourth powers return 16cisπ.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: When finding roots, include all k=0,…,n−1, not just a calculator principal root. For z=0 there is exactly one distinct root, namely 0.

blocks.prompt: How many distinct cube roots does a nonzero complex number have?
blocks.explanation: For nonzero input, the three angles differ by 120°, producing three distinct roots.
